Jestina Mukoko

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Jestina Mukoko

Abducted from her home by the CIO in 2008, Jestina Mokuko is lucky to be alive – As a co founder of the Zimbabwe peace project she was accused of being an enemy of the state. The trumped up charges included trying to recruit a single policemen to over throw the ZANU PF government. She was accused of helping the MDC with recruitment. It’s a story that can also be a warning of what happens in a one party state when the democratic institutions there to protect individual freedoms break down.
Jestina was tortured for days at a time – hit on the soles of her feet with a truncheon and pipe. She was blindfolded and kept in solitary confinement. She was made to kneel on stones till she says the pain was so bad, she left her body and watched the proceedings from the ceiling. Later she was moved to Chikurubi before being released. Her trial in which advocate Jeremy Gauntlet came to her defence was packed with journalists, human rights activists and even diplomats. His defence was based on the following points:
no warrant of arrest

subjection to inhuman and degrading treatment

unlawful detention

solitary confinement

torture

threats of harm

deprivation of medical care

deprivation of access to a lawyer

connivance between the police and state security agents

Further information:
When she disappeared it is likely that only the international pressure placed on the ZANU PF government saved her. At the time hundreds of activists were going missing and ended up dead.

2008 was a terrible year in Zimbabwe – people were literally starving, 4000 people died of cholera, inflation was so bad that the value of money on a morning was more than the value that same evening. In Chikerubi the prisoners formed friendships with some of their guards who would spend their days trying to get food for their families and come in for night duty and tell the prisoners that they were sleeping. The prisoners would keep watch for their captors. Sometimes they would sing hymns together. It was a strange time. After the courts found in her favour she suffered from post traumatic stress and it was thanks largely to a South African doctor that she was able to return to a normal life.

AN EXCERPT
With my passport back I travelled to several parts of the world. First I went to the USA, where I was invited to present a paper at Syracuse University and was honoured to meet the then US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and the First Lady, Michelle Obama. I also travelled to Ireland, where I met the teams that had campaigned for my release and I attended mass with the congregation in Belfast that had dedicated prayers for me.
To celebrate International Human Rights Day in 2009 the City of Weimer in Germany handed me the Human Rights Prize and, while I was away the National Association of Non-Governmental Organisations in Zimbabwe awarded me the Peace Prize for 2009. In March 2010 I received the US Secretary of State International Women of Courage Award. At the ceremony in the US I was asked to make the acceptance speech for all ten of the women who were honoured – only two of them from Africa. The honour was, for me, the icing on the cake.
During my travels I realised that I represented many people who face injustice, but most of all I saw myself representing the multitude of committed Zimbabweans who were demanding that human rights be respected.
At the beginning of 2010 I accepted an offer of specialised psychological treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder at the Denmar Clinic in Pretoria, South Africa. Takudzwa, who had decided to take a gap year after his A levels (Advanced level examinations) to be with me, joined me in sessions therapy with Dr Steenkamp, which went on for six weeks. During those six weeks he could not hide his joy. ‘Mama, I am so happy you are the mother that I know and I am enjoying your cooking that I had gone without for such a long time.’
The ordeal and the events subsequent to it had caused us to drift apart, overwhelmed, at times, by attention from friends and relatives.
During our time in Pretoria we had time to bond and he opened up about his feelings, anxieties and fears during the time that I was away. On my birthday in March 2011 the French Embassy in Harare announced that I had been awarded the Légion d’Honneur, which dates back to Napoleon’s time.
Jestina continues her work with the ZIMBABWE PEACE PROJECT. She is a former news anchor at ZBC.

Press Release:


Jestina Mukoko
Abducted from her home, interrogated, tortured and later dumped in Zimbabwe’s notorious Chikurubi prison, Jestina Mukoko is lucky to be alive. As the brave co-founder of the Zimbabwe Peace Project, Jestina was accused of trying to overthrow the Zanu-PF government, in a time when hundreds of activists were disappearing and ending up dead. Today she has garnered international accolades for her work as an activist, culminating in an autobiography on her fight for human rights in Zimbabwe. In a poignant interview, Jestina tells Carte Blanche how she became the ultimate enemy of the state.


Script:


JESTINA MUKOKO FINAL SCRIPT TX Sunday 24th April 2016

Commentary One
Jestina Mukoko has just returned from a visit to the White House, where women of courage from around the world were honoured. Jestina is a defender of human rights in Zimbabwe. A dangerous place to take on the ruling state.

Jestina Mukoko
I never imagined that I would be a victim one day – I did not think that the work I was doing was going to make people so angry, as to want me dead!

Commentary Two
Jestina was well known in Zimbabwe. She had once been a news anchor at ZBC. Then in 2007 she became the director of Zimbabwe Peace project.

Jestina
The Zimbabwe Peace Project monitors and documents human rights violations.

Commentary Three
Early morning. December 3rd 2008. Jestina was abducted from her home in Norton, 40kms west of Harare. She was still in her nightdress and dressing gown, when she was bundled into an unmarked car and disappeared

LINK
She was driven blindfolded at high speed with her abductors, and was dumped in what she thought was a pantry. Jestina would spend twenty- one days in there.

Jestina
You can go insane. You hear voices that are non- existent. I heard my name called out, and when I was not using my dressing gown as a blind fold I also tried to use it to keep me sane I would remove threads from it to keep me sane

Commentary Four
That morning in SA, another defender of human rights, Elinor Sisulu got the e mails. Jestina’s son had alerted her networks, minutes after she disappeared

Elinor Sisulu
I didn’t believe I would ever see her again. In that moment I cried as if she had died.

Commentary Five
Elinor says 2008 was Zimbabwe’s annus Horriblis. 4000 people died of cholera. The shops were empty, there was hyperinflation, and hundreds of people opposed to the regime, were abducted. Some disappeared

Elinor Sisulu
I literally remember that people dropped everything. We did all this with urgency,
If the longer they have disappeared the less likely you find them alive

Jestina
There were all these angels and they became a force to reckon with

Commentary six
But the politics were against her. It was a time of President Mbeki’s quiet diplomacy

Elinor Sisulu
And that quiet diplomacy the thing that we were very critical about is that it tried as far as possible to silence the conversation about human rights abuses

LINK
In Zimbabwe its known as Falanga, a form of torture that is not supposed to leave a trace, basically Jestina was hit on the souls of her feet until she thought they would burst.

JESTINA
I realized if I continued screaming they were going to have satisfaction so I decided I was going to withstand the pain
Claire
Was it an act of defiance?
Jestina
I think so – My son said I feared they would kill you because you are stubborn

Commentary Seven
Alone and terrified, Jestina faced the Central Intelligence Organisation who wanted to know why she was travelling to Botswana

Jestina
They were now saying you regularly travel to Botswana because you work with MDC where you are recruiting young people, to come back to Zimbabwe and overthrow a constitutionally elected government that was a surprise to me because all the travels were basically to buy foodstuffs

Claire
Were you protecting people or did you have that information to share
Jestina
I wasn’t protecting anyone …what they didn’t tell me was that they wanted to muzzle the work of the organization

Commentary eight
She was accused of recruiting a single policeman to overthrow the government

Elinor Sisulu
I think it was to terrorize and intimidate MDC and arms dealing and guerilla movement so anybody who was opposed to the government armed insurrection supported by the west

Commentary nine
And they made her sign a bogus admission and threatened her with death



Jestina
I think the exact words were you have a choice of becoming a state witness or become extinct and if you go extinct we can bury you around this building
Claire
And you had heard digging outside?
Jestina
I thought that must be my grave being dug

Commentary Ten
In the interrogation room mounds of sand were prepared for Jestina to kneel on

Jestina
He told me to kneel on it. The pain was so intense it numbed me and found myself drifting from this body and watching this woman suffer from up there that is what that pain did to me

Commentary eleven
After a week she was driven blindfolded to her abductors bosses in the middle of the day
Jestina
I was being driven around Harare in blindfolds and no one noticed

Commentary twelve
When she arrived she was allowed to sit in a chair for the first time.
Jestina
I was given a chair my heart nearly left my chest
Why?
I thought I was on the chair where they would kill me

Commentary thirteen
But here the torture was more psychological

Jestina
One of the men said where did you leave your son and his next question was is he still at home as a mother I thought I had failed in my role

Commentary Fourteen
After she disappeared Jestina’s brother Cosmas began a grisly search in the mortuaries
Jestina
He started on this dark journey he believed that I had been killed and he wanted his sister to have a decent burial

Commentary Fifteen
Elinor wasn’t alone in applying pressure, Amnesty international, Zimbabwe lawyers for human rights, and many others across the world applied pressure at the highest level.



LINK
No one really knows if the international pressure played a role, but Jestina suddenly appeared in court. She was charged with terrorism and while the charges were bad enough the leg irons were the ultimate humiliation

Jestina
My son was sitting in with his uncles, I couldn’t look him in the eye. I had been degraded as a mother and there my son was sitting watching his mother trudging into a court like a hard core criminal. It was a terrible experience

Commentary sixteen
Elinor Sisulu was appalled by the trial.
Elinor
It was absolutely shocking. The performance of the magistrate it was embarrassing …you could see there was no case

LINK
Still Jestina was not free she was incarcerated for another 50 days in Chikerubi.

Commentary seventeen
Jestina weighed 80 kilograms when she was abducted, and 52 kilograms when she went into Chikerubi

Jestina
I think what was painful at Chikerubi …reduced to a number and they would call you by your number and they would not use your name they would use your number

Commentary eighteen
Her case was then referred to the Constitutional court

Jestina
There was a huge crowd I could here my brother shouting we are here for you.

Commentary nineteen
Ten months after her arrest Jestina Mukoko was acquitted, but she struggled to return to normal life

Jestina
I had become different person, I had so much anger in me, so much pain

Commentary twenty
And she obsessively looked for people in blindfolds being driven across Harare.

Jestina
My driver would ask have you seen someone you know, but I was looking for people with blindfolds




Commentary Twenty- One
Jestina warned that what happened to her could happen again

Up sound Jestina
If an opportunity comes what do you think will happen?

And a year ago Human rights activist Itai Dsamara was abducted and has not been seen since. Jestina still lives in Zimbabwe and hopes one day to help establish a TRC in that country

THE END duration 10 mins.

Promo one 15 seconds
Zimbabwe human rights activist Jestina Mukoko was in South Africa this week to launch her new book
Jestina
I thought I was now sitting on the chair where they would kill me

Promo Two 15 seconds
Jestina Mukoko relates her story of abduction and torture
Jestina
The pain was so intense it numbed me and found myself drifting from this body

Promo 10 seconds
Despite being abducted, tortured, & thrown into Chikerubee prison, Jestina Mukoko is still speaking out against Zimbabwean human rights violations

The pain was so intense it numbed me and found myself drifting from this body and watching this woman suffer from up there that is what that pain did to me Commentary eleven After a week she was driven blindfolded to her abductors bosses in the middle of the day Jestina I was being driven around Harare in blindfolds and no one noticed Commentary twelve When she arrived she was allowed to sit in a chair for the first time. Jestina I was given a chair my heart nearly left my chest Why? I thought I was on the chair where they would kill me Commentary thirteen But here the torture was more psychological Jestina One of the men said where did you leave your son and his next question was is he still at home as a mother I thought I had failed in my role Commentary Fourteen After she disappeared Jestina’s brother Cosmas began a grisly search in the mortuaries Jestina He started on this dark journey he believed that I had been killed and he wanted his sister to have a decent burial Commentary Fifteen Elinor wasn’t alone in applying pressure, Amnesty international, Zimbabwe lawyers for human rights, and many others across the world applied pressure at the highest level. LINK No one really knows if the international pressure played a role, but Jestina suddenly appeared in court. She was charged with terrorism and while the charges were bad enough the leg irons were the ultimate humiliation Jestina My son was sitting in with his uncles, I couldn’t look him in the eye. I had been degraded as a mother and there my son was sitting watching his mother trudging into a court like a hard core criminal. It was a terrible experience Commentary sixteen Elinor Sisulu was appalled by the trial. Elinor It was absolutely shocking. The performance of the magistrate it was embarrassing …you could see there was no case LINK Still Jestina was not free she was incarcerated for another 50 days in Chikerubi. Commentary seventeen Jestina weighed 80 kilograms when she was abducted, and 52 kilograms when she went into Chikerubi Jestina I think what was painful at Chikerubi …reduced to a number and they would call you by your number and they would not use your name they would use your number Commentary eighteen Her case was then referred to the Constitutional court Jestina There was a huge crowd I could here my brother shouting we are here for you. Commentary nineteen Ten months after her arrest Jestina Mukoko was acquitted, but she struggled to return to normal life Jestina I had become different person, I had so much anger in me, so much pain Commentary twenty And she obsessively looked for people in blindfolds being driven across Harare. Jestina My driver would ask have you seen someone you know, but I was looking for people with blindfolds Commentary Twenty- One Jestina warned that what happened to her could happen again Up sound Jestina If an opportunity comes what do you think will happen? And a year ago Human rights activist Itai Dsamara was abducted and has not been seen since. Jestina still lives in Zimbabwe and hopes one day to help establish a TRC in that country THE END duration 10 mins. Promo one 15 seconds Zimbabwe human rights activist Jestina Mukoko was in South Africa this week to launch her new book Jestina I thought I was now sitting on the chair where they would kill me Promo Two 15 seconds Jestina Mukoko relates her story of abduction and torture Jestina The pain was so intense it numbed me and found myself drifting from this body Promo 10 seconds Despite being abducted, tortured, & thrown into Chikerubee prison, Jestina Mukoko is still speaking out against Zimbabwean human rights violations Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Jestina Mukoko (4768) Joy Summers 25 April 2016

metadata.Summary: Jestina Mukoko Abducted from her home by the CIO in 2008, Jestina Mokuko is lucky to be alive – As a co founder of the Zimbabwe peace project she was accused of being an enemy of the state. The trumped up charges included trying to recruit a single policemen to over throw the ZANU PF government. She was accused of helping the MDC with recruitment. It’s a story that can also be a warning of what happens in a one party state when the democratic institutions there to protect individual freedoms break down. Jestina was tortured for days at a time – hit on the soles of her feet with a truncheon and pipe. She was blindfolded and kept in solitary confinement. She was made to kneel on stones till she says the pain was so bad, she left her body and watched the proceedings from the ceiling. Later she was moved to Chikurubi before being released. Her trial in which advocate Jeremy Gauntlet came to her defence was packed with journalists, human rights activists and even diplomats. His defence was based on the following points: no warrant of arrest subjection to inhuman and degrading treatment unlawful detention solitary confinement torture threats of harm deprivation of medical care deprivation of access to a lawyer connivance between the police and state security agents
metadata.Further information: When she disappeared it is likely that only the international pressure placed on the ZANU PF government saved her. At the time hundreds of activists were going missing and ended up dead. 2008 was a terrible year in Zimbabwe – people were literally starving, 4000 people died of cholera, inflation was so bad that the value of money on a morning was more than the value that same evening. In Chikerubi the prisoners formed friendships with some of their guards who would spend their days trying to get food for their families and come in for night duty and tell the prisoners that they were sleeping. The prisoners would keep watch for their captors. Sometimes they would sing hymns together. It was a strange time. After the courts found in her favour she suffered from post traumatic stress and it was thanks largely to a South African doctor that she was able to return to a normal life. AN EXCERPT With my passport back I travelled to several parts of the world. First I went to the USA, where I was invited to present a paper at Syracuse University and was honoured to meet the then US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and the First Lady, Michelle Obama. I also travelled to Ireland, where I met the teams that had campaigned for my release and I attended mass with the congregation in Belfast that had dedicated prayers for me. To celebrate International Human Rights Day in 2009 the City of Weimer in Germany handed me the Human Rights Prize and, while I was away the National Association of Non-Governmental Organisations in Zimbabwe awarded me the Peace Prize for 2009. In March 2010 I received the US Secretary of State International Women of Courage Award. At the ceremony in the US I was asked to make the acceptance speech for all ten of the women who were honoured – only two of them from Africa. The honour was, for me, the icing on the cake. During my travels I realised that I represented many people who face injustice, but most of all I saw myself representing the multitude of committed Zimbabweans who were demanding that human rights be respected. At the beginning of 2010 I accepted an offer of specialised psychological treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder at the Denmar Clinic in Pretoria, South Africa. Takudzwa, who had decided to take a gap year after his A levels (Advanced level examinations) to be with me, joined me in sessions therapy with Dr Steenkamp, which went on for six weeks. During those six weeks he could not hide his joy. ‘Mama, I am so happy you are the mother that I know and I am enjoying your cooking that I had gone without for such a long time.’ The ordeal and the events subsequent to it had caused us to drift apart, overwhelmed, at times, by attention from friends and relatives. During our time in Pretoria we had time to bond and he opened up about his feelings, anxieties and fears during the time that I was away. On my birthday in March 2011 the French Embassy in Harare announced that I had been awarded the Légion d’Honneur, which dates back to Napoleon’s time. Jestina continues her work with the ZIMBABWE PEACE PROJECT. She is a former news anchor at ZBC.
